'fhe Grand Master then delivered his Annual Address to the Grand
Lodge of California, as follows:BBETIIREX OF THE GRAND LoDGE OF CALIFORXIA !
Among the expected events ever Lefore ns in the flight of time, which _the heart
fondly anticipates as we near the point of fruition, is the Annual Convocatrnn of the
Grand Lodge of Masons, to those of the Craft who have parted 011 the square and
traveled upon tbe level through the vicissitudes of a passing ye!\r •.
Since last we separated, mauly aspirations, no doubt, h:we exmteil each of us to
deeds of energY.and enterprise-to exertions in the battle of life, ":here some have.won
the meed desired, and others, perhaps, have wearied by the way, m trouble and disappointment. Our farewell was uttered in the true _sentiment of hr.oth_erhood, ~nil,as we
parted, each one on his path of life, the strong bgaments of af!ecti~n betw~en .heart
and heart have held us in sympathy ia our wanderings, warmed us mto action for the
fulfillment of our missions, and finally brought us together again in the satisfactory as·
surance that our progress, as Masons, bas been onward and triumphant. Let our first
earnest desire be, in this happy Ieunion, that it may so continue through all the ages
the historv of our Order may chronicle ; and then, let us, in unity of purpose, act our
parts to~rds the preservation· of the 'l'emple which has sheltered us, and which we
hope may shelter those who will live in that far-off era when our names and our
.
times will only be known as part of the record of a glorious past.
I welcome von upon this occasion, brethren of the Grand Lodge, with all the feeling a.nd symp;thy of a heart long accustomed ~o appreciate the true val~e and import·
ance of a friendship springing from the best impulses of our nature, directed by the
mystic intelligibility .of our Craft, and coequal in duration with the life ~f Masons.
I am once more permitted to congratulate you upon the general prosperity of the
Fraternity in this jurisdiction, a.nd up<ln the good order, harmony, and unequalled sue·

[May 14,

Immediately after the close of the last .Annual Commnnication, the usual letters
of authorization to constitute the eight new Lodges then chartered, were issued by
me ; and in due time all were returned to the office of the Grand Secretary, with the
proper reports by the several Grand Officers and Past Masters to whom they were
addressed. The names, numbers, and locations of these Lodges will be found at
page 380 of the printed proceedings of last year, and tl1e letters and reports will
be submitted by the proper officer.
In the month of December, 1859, the hall and all the property of Windsor Lodge,
N 0 • ll6, at Windsor, in Sierra County, were destroyed by fire; and on the seventh
day of July, 1860, a majority of its members assembled for the first time after that
event, when, in consequence of this great loss, of inability to procure a suitable placo
of meeting, and of a j]iminished membership occasioned by numerous removals, it,
was unanimously declared to be inexpedient to attempt a continuation of labor, and
a resolution was adopted requesting the Grand Lodge to accept a surrender of the
charter. A return of its membership, together with sundry communications in ref·
erence to the affairs of the Lodge, are ou file in the Grand Secretary's office, which
will be by him presented to you. Under these circumstances, I recommend that
the surrender of the charter be accepted, and that the Grand Secretary be authorized
to issue the usual certificates of good standing to those who composed the f,odge.
Since our last .Annual Communication, I have issued seven dispensations to open
and hold new Lodges, the names and locations of which will be furnished you in the
report of the Grand Secretary. Upon a careful examination of their work, if it meets
your approval, I recommend that charters be granted them. I have also issued
twenty.six special dispensations during the past year. Of these, twenty-two authorized a re ballot upon rejected petitions for degrees; three authorized elections at
times other than the general one provided in the Constitution; and one authorized the
conferring of the third degree at a period earlier than that permitted by the By-Laws
of the Lodge requesting it. The petitions for all these, setting forth in full the
reasons for the applications, are on file in the Gram1 Secretary's office, and will be
submitted for your examination.
The fifth Annual Report of the Masonic Board of Relief of the City of San Fran·
eisco will be presented to you by the Chairman of that Board; and I again take the
occasion to say, that too much praise can not be bestowed upon our brethren of that
city for their noble efforts in behalf of the affticted and destitute in their hour of need.
A communication has been received from our brethren of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21,' at
Honolulu, in the Hawaiian Islands, exhibiting a zeal and earnestness in the discharge
of their Masonitr' duties which entitles them to our highest commendation. It is a
source of pleasure to know that the most intimate fraternal relations now exist
between that Lodge and the Lodge Le Progres de l'Ooeani£, (at the same place, but
working under another jurisdiction,) and that they vie with each other only in noble
deeds of benevolence and charity. They earnestly and cordially invite one or all of
the Grand officers to visit them in their island home.
Before retiring from the high position of Grand Master, I must again be permitted
t-0 return you my heartfelt thanks for the forbearance, kindness, and courtesy which
I have ever received at your hands; and to ask that you join me in earnest prayer for
the perpetuity of our beloved ,Order, and that its blessed infiuences may be felt and
appreciated in all time and in every relation of human life.
N. GRE~JNE CURTIS, Grand Master.

and it is hoped tha~, ere long, all will consent to a uniformity so greatly to be desired.
The edition of the Constitution and Regulations ordered to be published in 1859,
having long since been exhausted, and it being probable that some amendments and
additions thereto will be adopted at this Communication, it is recommended that the
publication of another edition of three or four thousand copies be authorized, for the
informa.tion and convenience of the Lodges and Masons of this jurisdiction.

The petitions, with the dimits of the petitioners, the recommendations of' the
neighboring chartered Lodges, the certificates as to the qualifications of the officers
proposed, and the other papers required by our laws, were all in due form, and are
herewith presented. These, with Franklin Lodge, at Ornisbo, Sacramento County,
the dispensation to which was continued in May last, make eight Lodges now existing under dispensation. One hundred and forty-two have receiveil charters from the
Grand Lodge of California, since its organization, of' which two have been transferred
to the Grand J,odge of Oregon, fourteen have surrendered their charters, and two
have suffered 1their revocation, as will appear in full in the "Registry of Lodges";
leaving at this time, one hundred and thirty-two Lodges in active existence within
the jurisdiction. Jn addition to these, fonr other Lodges have had a brief existence
under dispensation, but, never having received clrnrters, they have not been continued in the registry, viz: Nashville Lodge, in 1851, at~ plucethenknown as Nashville,
in Mariposa County; Pacific Lodge, in 1853, at Valparaiso, in the Republic of Chile;
Folsom Lodge, in 1857, at Folsom, in Sacramento County; and Napa City Lodge, in
1858, at Napa City, in Napa County.
At the close of the fiscal year, on the first day of March, 181.il, there were bul·
ances standing against sundry Lodges for dues of 1860, amounting in all, to $158.
Of this amount, nearly all has been paid since that date, and the credits therefor will
appear in the accounts of the current year. The Lodges still delinquent are Santa
Clara, No. 34, for $30, and Sotoyomi, No. 123, for $4; and they are mentioned here,
not because any doubt exists as to their ability or willingness to cancel their indebtedness, but because the Constitution directs the undersigned to report such cases.
It is certainly gratifying to be enabled to record a fact so creditable to the Lodges of
this jurisdiction, as that so trifling a sum stands to their de bit upon the Grand Secretary's books, especially when that too is certain to be paid.

From the foregoing it will be seen that the amount disbursed by the Board since
its organization in 1856, is $16,700 30; of which sum $16,362 51 have been expended
directly for charitable purposes, and $337 79 for sundry unavoidable expenses. During
the year seven widows have received a regular monthly stipend of from ten dollars
to'twenty·five dollars each, some of them being far advanced in years, and able to
do but little for their own support.
In conclusion we again express our acknowledgment of indebtedness to the Cal·
ifornia Steam Navigation Company for its continued liberality in transporting upon
its .boats, free of charge, all those who have been recommended by this Board,thus adding largely to its means of assisting the needy and distressed ; and, if the customary meed of thanks to the Pacific Mail Steamship Company does not this year appear in our report, it is not because of any lack of willingness to be charitable on
the part of the agents of that company, Messrs. FORBES and BABCOCK, (both of whom
have often contributed to aid in paying for passages of the destitute,) but in conse·
quence of the stringent orders of their employers to take no passenger at less than
the .established rates.
All which is respectfully submitted by order of the Board.
JAMES LAIDLEY, Chairman.
GEORGE c. HICKOX, Secretary.

Bro. JAMES L. J<jNGLISH, from the Committee on Correspondence, prethe following report:--

~ented

To the N:. w.-. Gmml Lodge of Calijbmia :When the announcement was made, ot the last Annual Communication of the
Grand Lodge, or the Committee Oil CorreRpundence for the present year, the
writer objected to the position assigned him, and, stating that he expected to be
absent from the State a considerable portion of' the year, desired to be excused from
~rving. The Grand Master, however, refused to grant the request, and insisted upon
the appointment. The writer, well aware that, even if in the State, the mnltiplieity
of his engagements would preclude the possibility of his doing justice to the subject
even if he was enabled to do any thing at all toward preparing a report, then stated
that if it was designed to depend upon him for snch a paper, the Grand Lodge might
expect that none would be forthcoming. '!'his, too, had no effect, and the name of
the writer was given to the l\Iasonic world as Chairman of the Committee on Corres·
pondence.
The unwillingness of the undersigned to accept the position did not arise from a
want of interest in the subject, or a disposition to avoid any labor which it was in his
power to perform, calculated to p~omote the prosperity of the Order; but from the fact
that his time is so much occupied with business matters, and his mind so much harassed
with perplexing and vexatious cares, that he well knew that he could give neither
time nor mind to the preparation of a report. And it has been, as he supposed it would
be. The Annual Communication of the Grand Lodge is near at hand, and nothing
has been done. A pile of published proccedingR, three feet and a half high, is to be
read and digested; whilst matters of business, requiring daily attention, can not be
neglected. '!'he thing can not be done; it is an impossiblity. But, what can be donP,
shall be, little though it be; and if the report is but meagre, and unworthy of tho
Gund Lodge of California, which has attained by its elaborate papers from this committee a proud distinction, let the fault be laid rather at the door of the Grand Master,
than at that of the writer.

The Committee on Masonic Law and Usage reported against a proposition to dispense with the committee of enquiry into the character of an applicant for the de·
greea; as also against a proposition to make it the duty of the Junior Warden of a
Lodge to prefer and prosecute all char)l'.es for unmasonic conduct. The report was ap·
proved by the Grand Lodge.
The same committee, to whom was referred a resolution declaring that any Mason,
engaged in the retail of ardent spirits, ~hon Id be reprimanded,. suspended, or expelled, reported "That the retail of ardent s11irits is demoralizing, no impartial observer of its consequences can doubt. That it is an employment, inconsistent with the moral principles
inculcated by Masonry, and that a Mason should not engage in keeping a dram· shop,
is equally clear. Bnt whether the Grand Lodge should make the general declaration that every Mason engaged therein should he subject to discipline as for umnasonic conduct, or leave the subordinate Lodges to take such action in each particu·
lar case, as its peculiar features may seem to demand, your committee regard as a
qaestion of legislative discretion, to be determined by the Grand Lodge, and not hy
them. They are of the opinion, however, that tlie latter course is most expedient."
This is the correct view to be takeri of the matter. Each case should be left to
the judgment of the Lodge having jurisdiction.

Masomc cnme, known and recognized by the common Jaw of the Order.
"If these views are correct, the only remaining question lJertinent to the present
issue is, whether the payment of fixed and regular Lodge dues is an intrinsic, essential, and original µart of Free Masonry.
"It is scarcely necessary to assert here, the fact so well understood ancl universally admitted, tl:iat until a very recent period, Jong after the establishment of subordinate Lodges,,no such thing as an assessment of dues was known. That period is
within the recollection of many of our older Masons, who must view with astonishment an effort to make what was originally a mere rule of convenience of a single
Lodge, the vital law of a wide-spread fraternity. But further, the requirement is not
general, much less uniform, even at this day. l\Iany of the Lodges in our own country are supported by the voluntary contribntious of their membcrn, or by revenue
dPl'ived from heavy initiation fees; ancl in onr own jurisdiction, where dues are universally required, their amount ranges from one dollar and a half to ten dollars per
annum.
"If, thon, this cluty is one of modern origin, of but partial enforcement, and of
irregular and arbitrary character, it can not certainly be regarded as an essential part
of Masonry, but merely as one of those responsihilities which the individual brother
assumes towards his own Lodge alone. In the language of Bro. Mackey, in his Principles of Masonic Law,' It is not an ohligation on the part of a Mason to the institution at large, but is in reality a specbl contrnct, in which the only parties are a particular Lodge and its members, of which the fraternity as a mass are to know notlnng.'
"~'or these reasons your committee are of opinion that the failure or neglect to
pay Lodge dues docs not constitute a lllasonic crime; that it is no breach of any general law of Masonry, an cl that therefore it can not, upon any just principle, warrunt the
infliction of a punishment upon the defa.ulting brother, which would disturb the relations existing between him ancl othcrn as members of the fraternity at large, or which
would deprive him of any purely Masonic privilege. They arc also of the opinion,
that the failure to comply with the requirements of the by-Jaws in this respect is such
a breach of the contract exi..;ting between the individual brother nnrl his Lodge as
,iustifies the termination 9f his mcmbcrnhip and his exclusion from all mere Lodge
privileges.
"Your committee are fully aware of several objections which have been and still
are urged a.gainst the view here taken, some of which it may not be improper to
notice.
"I. It is claimed that the failure by a member to pay the required dues, amounts to
~mch a violation of his cluty to observe tl:ie by-laws as should subject him to the penalty of suspension. Without placing any stress npon the fact that, at the time of his
admission to the Louge, a Master ~foson can not know all, nor in dee cl many of the requirements of the by-laws, it will be SL1fficient, in order to show the fallacy of the
urgument, to point out some other requirements usually found in them, disobedience
to which would, on the principle claimed, as certainly justify the penalty of suspension, as the offence now under consideration. As, for example, it is made the cluty,
respecth·ely, of the officers to attend all meetings of the Lodge; of the Secretary to
keep-certain books in a prescribed form; of the members of committees to report
within specified periods; of the 'l'ylcr to kcev the furniture of the Loclge in good ·
order, &c. Now, as far as an infraction of the by-laws is concerned, a failure to
perform either of these duties is as definite an offence as the failure to pay dues, inasmuch as they are all required by the same instrument, and under precisely the same
sanction; but can it be conceived that a neglect of them could 1rnssibly be constrned
into so grave an offence as to subject the otl'ender to the penalty of suspension from
Masonry?
"2. It is argue cl, that the failure to pay the uues required, is a wrong done the Lodge,
and as such, constitutes a mnch highe1· offence, and deserves a much more severe
punishment than has been indicated. If, however, this be true, then the same construction wonld establish a criterion by which to judge of the relations existing between individual Masons, and would thus create a grade of Masonic crime which has
never as yet been suggested. Wherever positive franc] is committed or attempted,
the party is guilty of a crime known and recognized by the fraternity, and should be
punisher! accordingly. But in the absence of any fraudulent intent, a failure to pay
can not be construed into a crime.
"3. It is said that a mere dropping a member from the rolls, or exc1udin" him from
Lodge privileges, is not such a penalty as will protect the Lodge and secure the objects
of a common fund. In replying to this obJection, your committee beg leave very
briefly to refer to another subject, which, although not specially in charge, is inti-

IOWA.
The Grand Lodge as"cmLled at Burlington, on T11esda.r, June fifth, 1860,-the .lf.·.
lV>. J. R. HARTSOCK' Grand Master' presiding.
A committee appointed at the previous session to report on the subject of non·
affiliation, made a lengthy report, in tJw course of whicl1, they say:"And again, to establish a mle that a non-affiliated Mason shall become a member
of a Lodge, must be placed in the same category 1dth, and may be termed cornpul·
sory }.Casonry, and for the reasons we have given above, can find no justification in
1rinciple, notwithstanding the expressed opinion of men, or the late actions of Grand
,odges upon this question of compulsory membership, or affiliation. Your commit·
tee have spent no time to inquire from whence originated the idea of compulsory
Masonry, or what prompted the action of Grand Lodges npon that subject-as they
believe it originated in the hair·brained imagination of Masons of modem iileas upon
that subject, and that the action of Urand Lodges have been premature, hasty, and
without much thought or investigation in relation to the important principles involved;
more the product of policy than principle. In fine, we may be indulged in saying
that cornp11lsory membership and compulsory affiliation may be termed the bantling,;
of modei·n progression and 'innovation, because we are well assured that the great
and benevolent principles of ancient Pree masonry justify no such thing as compulsory
Masonry. And while your committee say tMs, they fully accord the sentiment and
admonition contained in the ' ancient charges.' ' that every Mason ought to be a mem·
ber of a Lodge,' yet the individual mnst be left free to determine that for himself, as
the ' ancient charge" is admonitory, and not mandatory-as it lays down no rule by
which a member of a Lodge can be compelled to remain, or one who is not a mem·
her can be compelled to join against his will, nor does the ancient charge impose
any penalty to enforce the one or the other-hence it leaves it to the option ol' the
Mason himself to determine in view of the obligations resting upon him.
"Therefore, our advice in relation to this vexed question is, cease to quarrel with
all such, let them go, and say to all such, if you will not perform Masonic work, we
will not feed you with Masonic foot1. 'l.'his you may do, in accordance with justice
and with propriety, as the Great, lAg/11; declares that he that will not work shall not
eat; more than this, you may refuse to permit non·alllliatcs to visit your Lodges, to
attend festivals, or to join processions, and refuse to them the rights of Masonic bur·
ial, &c. But in our opinion the ancient usages and prineiJiles of Masonry will not
allow you to hold a member of a Louge who is in good standing (whose dnes are paid
when he desires to <limit,) against his will when lie i8 not in debt to the Lodge, nor
compel him to remain when he desires to dimit. Nor can you in view of'the principle~
of Masonry as anciently uuderstooil, compel a non-affiliated Mason to become a melll·
ber- but must leave it to his own discretion, without compulsion or coercion.''
It was decided that the thirty·nine regulations, adopted in 1721, when }fr. GEORGE
PAYNE was Grand }faster of Englanu, are not, and at no time have been in force in this
jurisdiction.

Proceedings of the

To the M. ·. W. ·. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom were referred the petition for a charter, and the recordbooks and other papers of Franklin Lodge, at Ornisbo, in Sacramento County, have
carefully examined the proceedings of said ·Lodge, and find them generally to conform to the requirements of our Constitution and General Regulations. They discover, however, that in several instances this Lodge has opened its stated communications on the first or second degree; deferring the approval of the minutes of the preceding stated communication until after the conferring of the first or second .degree,
as the case might be.. This your committee deem an irregularity, believing that the
stated communication should always be opened on the third degree, and that the first
· business transacted should be the approval of the minutes of the preceding stated
and called communications.
Your committee also find that on one occasion the Lodge called off a stated communication for two weeks, to a time other than the next stated communication, and
at that time transacted business. 'r11is also is an irregularity, and contrary to the
provisions of the Constitution of this Grand Lodge. Believing, however, that the
brethren erred with no intention to violate the law, and that the errors above mentioned will not be repeated, your committee offer the following resolution for adoption: Resolved, That a charter be granted to }i'ranl;lfo Lodge, at Ornisbo, in Sacramento
County, and that it be numbered according to the date of its dispensation.
All which is respectfully submitted.
E. Il. VAN DIWAH,

worthy a purpose shall not go unrewarded.
Several <Jnestions aro propounded in the communication of Bro. MARS1IAJ,L, of
which but ouo 11ppears to require notice. It is asked whether, when a Muson dies, he
is entitled to Masonic burial ; am! if so, whether a single individual must bear the expense? A deceased sojourning brother, who was in good standing, is certainly entitled to Masonic burial; and if an individual renders that last service, he may well
ask that his brethreu and neighbors help him to bear the burden, if so it appears to
him to be. But he can scarcely demand this al'! 11 right. lie has done his duty, and
they ought to be willing to assist him ; but let him not detract from the merit of his
charity by his complainings. Go<! lovoth a cheerful giver.

To the M. •• W.·. Grand Lodge of California :You:r committee, to whom was referred .the memorial of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21,
at Honolulu, in the Hawaiian Islands, respectfully report thereon as follows :After due consideration of the appeal made by Bros. CLARK, FoRNANDER, and
MONTGOMERY, the committee acting in behalf of said Lodge, your committee are
unanimously of the opinion that a remission of its dues, in accordance with the
prayer of the memorialists, should be cheerfully granted. The peculiar position of
our mid-ocean subordinate of necessity subjects it to continued calls, not only upon
its treasury, but upon the individual liberality of its members, nod that too in much
larger sums than are usually demanded from the Lodges under this jurisdiction; and
the memorial now presented to you, with others which have preceded it, afford con·
vincing proof that our brethren of Hawaiian Lodge have set an example of liberal·
ity which it may well become this Grand Lodge to imitate.
The cordial invitation extended to our Grand Officers to visit our brethren of Hon·
olulu, your committee deem well worthy of attention, and they urge the propriety of
a compliance with the request by some one or more of the elective officers of this
Grand Lodge. Such a visit would doubtless redound to the interest of the fraternity
residing in that insulated part of our jurisdiction; would convince that portion of
it immediately allied to us that distance has not had power to separate its members
from our memories; would afford an opportunity to inspect their work, and, if necessary, to correct it so that it should correspond with that ordained by this Grand
Lodge ; and could not fail to be most pleasant and happy for those accepting the in·
vitation. The pleasure so eloquently presented as anticipated by the memorialists,
should their request in this respect be acceded to, shows how hospitably ~uch a visitor or visitors would be received and entertained; and your committee express the
urgent hope that some prominent officer of this Grand Lodge will take an early opportunity, by availing himself of this invitation, to give himself much enjoyment, and
to prove to our Hawaiian brethren that we affectionately remember our ocean child.
In conclusion, your committee, consulting their own inclinations as well as obeying the mandate of the Grand Lodge, ·offer the following resolution for adoption:Resolved, That the dues of Hawaiian Lodge, No. 21, for the year ending March 1,
1861, be and are hereby remitted.
All which is respectfully submitted.
CHARLES MARSH, )
ISAAC s. TITUS,

In 1860, Los Angele.~ Lodge petitioned this Grand Body for the restoration of Mr.
RUBOTTOM, and the Committee on Jurisprndence, to whom that petition was referredas an act of courtesy to the Grand Lodge of Arkansas-recommended th11t the attention of that Grand Lodge he again called to the subject, and that no further action be
had thereon until the present Communication.
Your committee are well aware of the Masonic law, that no authority can restore
a Mason,.expelled for unmasonic conduct, other than that which inflicted the penalty;
provided, always, the case was fully under its jurisdiction. In this instance, however,
Mr. RUBOTTOM had received his <limit from the Lodge at a time when all the facts of
the unfortunate occurrence upon which the charges preferred against him were
based, were fully known, and had left the State of Arkansas with the avowed purpose
of removing to and becoming a resident of California; a state of circumstances,
which, as your committee think, did not leave to Franklin Lodge, No. 9, any right
of jurisdiction in the case.
Your committee are of the opinion, therefore, that-considering all the facts, Lear- .
ing in mind the Jong delay in making what appears to be a just reparation, a delay
caused by our strong desire not only not to be, but not to seem to be discourteous
to the Grand Lodge of Arkansas, and recollecting that a prominent committee of that
body have, in effect, expressed views in consonance with our own-this Grand Lodge
may well act upon this case, and that justice requires it to do so at this Communion·
tion ; and to that end they recommend the adoption of the following resolution:-

Resolved, That W. W. RUBOTTOM. heretofore excluded from the Lodges in this
jurisdiction, be restored to all the rights and privileges of Masonry.
All which is respectfully submitted.
WILLIAM C. BELCHER,

Bro. WM. 0. BELCHER, from the special committee appointed to examine the Record Book of 1.'uolumne Lodi;(e, No. 81 present-ad the following
roport:'fu the ,"tf.·. W:. Grand Lodge of California :Your committee, to whom the Book of Hecords of Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8, was
referred for examination, respectfully report that they have carefully examined those
records, and find thel'ein irregularities of such a character as, in their opinion, de·
nmnd the prompt and decided action of this Grand Lodge.
From them it appears that two meetings of the Lodge were held at which neither
ihe MaHter nor either of his Wardens was present- one a special meeting on the ninth
1lay of J 1me, 1860, at which Bro. E. G. LYONS received the I'ellow Craft degree -the
other a·stated meeting on the third day of November, 1860, at which important busi·
ness was transacted, with only five members of the Lodge present. On the fourth
dn.y of August, 1860, J. HAlDillL petitioned the Lodge for the degrees ol' Masonry. It
11ppearing that his residence was within the jurisdiction of Gem·ge Wasli:ington Lodge,
No. 62, action upon his petition was deferred, and the Secretary was directed to ask
permission of that Lodge to receive the petition, and confer the degrees upon the ap·
plicant. Gem·ge Washington Lodge refused such permission, but before the refusal
was known to Tuolumne Lodge, the petition was received and referred to a committee,

[May 18,

Bro. W.W. TRAYLOR at the time calling the attention of the Lodge to the question
of jurisdiction and protesting against its action. At the meeting of November third,
1860, only one member of the committee to whom the petition had been referred
being present, and the Lodge having been informed of the refusal of George Wash·
ingUm Lodge, two other members were added to the committee, and instructed to
report immediately. They did so report, and Mr. HAMMEL was elected to receive the
degrees of Masonry in that Lodge. At the same meeting, no member of the committee
appointed upon the petition of Bro. YouNT for affiliation, (presented and referred at a
previous meeting,) being present, a new committee was appointed and instructed to
report immediately, which they did, and Bro. YOUNT was elected a member of Tuolmnne Lodge. At the two meetings of the Lodge referred to, Bro. Cius. M. RADCLIFF,
the present Jlfaster, and a Past Grand Master of this State, presided; and your com·
mittee learn, from the testimony of members of the Lodge, that the Senior Warden,
Bro. EmroNDSON, (who was the proper custodian of the charter, the Master being ab·
sent from the county,) on the evening of November third, 1860, refused to deliver the
charter to any other person to open the Lodge, and that while he was engaged in a
public procession, that instrument was sent for and obtained from his wife.
Your committee feel great delicacy in censuring tlie acts of a Past Grand Master,
especially when that censure involves the charging him with a willful violation of the
Constitution and Regulations of our Grand Lodge ; but the record is before them,
and the duty assigned them must be performed. The exalted position formerly occupied by Bro. RADCLIFF, and the acquaintance with Masonic law and usage which
that position presupposes, render the irregularities of the Lodge, while under his di·
rection, of a much graver character than they would have been under one less skilled.
It is well settled that the Master, or one of his Wardens, must be present at every
meeting of the Lodge. The jurisdiction of Lodges, too, is well established and well
understood in California, and, in this instance, was distinctly brought to the knowl·
edge of the Lodge. Bro. RADCLIFF being present, and assuming to preside, the
jurisdictional rights of Ge01·ge Washin9ton Lodge, No. 62, were invaded, he, and the
Lodge, knowing that that Lodge, for reasons that seemed to it sufficient, had refosed
permission to receive the petition of the applicant. It is true that an order was
made, directing the Secretary to notiiy George Washin9ton Lodge that the fee for
the initiation of Mr. HAJJ)!EL was subject to its order, but that can not in any manner
relieve 'l'uolumne Lodge, and all who participated in its action in this matter, from
censure. It was the prhilege and the right of Geor9e Washington Lodge to give or
withhold its assent to the request preferred ; and Tuo"f:umne Lodge trespassed n11on
that right with full knowledge that such assent had been specifically refused.
At its last Annual Communication, this Grand Lodge decided that seven members
of a Lodge were necessary for the transaction of business; and your committee are
fully satisfied that tl1is regulation was distinctly understood and knowingly disregarded
by Bro. RADCLIFF, when assuming to preside at the nieeting of November third.
On the twentieth day of January, 1861, at a special meeting, a Lodge of Master
Masons was opened, at which the usual ceremonies of opening were waived. .A.
Master may, if he choose, omit a portion of the usual ceremony of opening or closing
a Lodge, but your committee nre not acquainted with the regulation which authorizes
an entire waiver of all these ceremonies.
The record of Bro. WEI:rnEER, the present Secretary of the Lodge, is very neatly
kept, and exhibits those qualities most desirable, if not indispensable, in a Secretarycare, judgment, and accuracy.
Your committee regret exceedingly that duty compels them to make a second unfavorable report on the records and transactions of Tuol·umne Lodge, and they are
Ratisfied that the censure for its irregularities should fall upon Bro. RADCLIFF rather
than upon the members of the Lodge ; for to him, as an old aud skillful Mason, one

1861.J

Grand Lodge of <Jalifornia.

75

who, for his knowledge and experience, had been raised to the highest honor in the
g!ft of the Fraternity, they might well look for advice and direction. He had made
mo.ny, perhaps most, of them Masons, and they might well look to him as a wise
counsellor upon whose judgment they could safely rely. Ignorance of the law is not
accounted good excuse for grave transgressions, .but it may entitle the transgressor
to a more favorable and merciful judgment than he could otherwise expect. Tuoi·
umne Lodge, in this case, has violated well known rules and regulations, and could
not well complain at the severest penalty which this Grand Body might infiict; but
your committee are of the opinion that its errors and transgressions are principally
chargeable to the unhappy guidance under which it has acted, and they are not
Inclined, at this time, to propose a further punishment for it than the str!'Ilg censure
herein meant to be recorded.
Bro. GEO. W. BAILEY, late Master of the Lodge, was absent from the county during
a considerable portion of his term of office, and the committee fully exonerate him
from all censure for the misguided and irregular proceedings of his Lodge.
Under the foregoing circumstances your committee deem it their duty to present,
and they do herewith present the following charges against Bro. CHAS. M. RADCLIFF,
now Master of Tuol·umne Lodge, No. 8, for unmasonic conduct, and the wilful viola·
tion of the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge of California, viz.:1st. That on the ninth day of June, lSGO, and on the third day of November, 1860,
he, assuming to act as llfaster, opened and presided over Tuolumne Lodge, No. 8,
when neither the Master nor either one of the Wardens of that Lodge was present.
2d. That, presiding in sucli a.~snmed character as Master, he, on the said third
day of November, 1860, allowed the business of the Lodge to be transacted when
only five members of the Lodge were present.
3d. That, presiding in such assumed character as llfaster, he, on the said third day
of November, 18GO, permitted, advised, and assisted in the election of an applicant
for the degrees of Jlfasonry, known to reside within the jurisdiction of George Wash·
in9ton Lodge, No. 62, and this, after the refusal of that Lodge to grant permission
had been commnnicated to him and to the Lodge.
4th. That, on f,he said third day of November, 1860, he obtained the charter of
that Lodge surreptltiously,-the Senior Warden, who was the proper custodian of
that instrument, (the llfaster being absent,) having refused to deliver the same to him,
or allow him, or any one else, to take it, and, under its authority, to open and hold
the Lodge on that evening.
5th. That, on the twentieth day of January, 1861, he, being then the Master ol'
said Lodge, dee.Jared his Lodge duly open and in order for business, by the authority
In him vested, waiving all ceremony, and without even inquiring of his Senior Warden
II' all present were Master Masons.
Your committee, in conclusion, offer the following resol11tions, and recommend
their adoption :- · ·

Bro. WM. C. BELCHER, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented
the following reports:Tu the .lf.-. W.·. Gl'and fodge of Oalifornia :Your committee, to whom were referred certain questions proposed by Bro.Joa!!
duty assigned them, and
respedfnlly submit the questions, with their opinions thereupon, as follows:QuestiOn 1st. Can a Lodge proceed to try a Master Mason, under suspension fot
non-payment of dues, for unmn.sonic conduct, without first restoring him?
.{inswer. It can; no matter what the cat1se of suspension may have been, it is
certainly within the power of a Lodge, having jurisdiction, to try a. suspended Mason
on charges of further unma~onic conduct, and to inflict such further punishment
It may deem proper.
Question 2d. Can a Lodge proceed to ti·y, for further unmasonic conduct, a Ma.son
suspended by itself, who,a.t the time charges are preferred against him, resides within
the jurisdiction of another Lodge, although the oft'ences charged were committed
while within the jurlsdiction of the Lodge first named?
Anl!Uler. It can not ; the proper course would be to prefer the charges before
the Lodge within whose jurisdiction the delinquent actually resides, by which he can
and should be tried. Prom the date of his suspension, whatever the cause thereof,
his membership in that Lodge ceases, and residence elsewhere carries with it juris·
diction.
All which is respectfully submitted.

We know that the institution we represent iR gootl. We, who lirwe stoorl within

numizing influences, that we neetl no statement of prcmi;;es, no logical deductions,

tho<c with liberal han<l. We believe that the institution is permanent. We l.ielicve
thli< hy our faith in the pcrm:incncy ot' gootl, !Jy om· faith that the structure that has
withstood storms so Jong-~o well---will not fall when the sky is clcnr ancl the storms
lmve passed away.
Rnt I can not finil in this individual cxperienei>, nor even in the long worthy past
or Masonry, nor in any of its qualities most apparrnt and most frequently adduced, a
loi.iical founrfation for. the faith we ban:' in it8 11biding permanency. ItR antiq11it.y
llwreases the esteem we liavc for it. It.< life commenced at an era unknown-hardly
1(1wsscd at. Its precepts, emblems, u.ncl ceremonic' have come clown tn tli• from
!.lutt olcl time, unchanged ancl unrccorde<l, by most mirncnlous tradition. Jt tencheH
hrntherly Jove, relief, and truth to-day, as it taught, l1ow many hund1·ed years ago Wl•
lrnow not-bearing through ages of violence and wrong, the hardy virtnes of nn n.p:c
of iron. Jt is no slmm, no work of a modem hand, buried in the earth to gather
mould, and labeled with the nnme of an old Ma•ter; but a veritable antique, bearing
t.hc undou!Jtctl, unqncstionahlc impre•.• of the centuries. l•'or this, we venerate arnl
love it. We hold it dearer in our heart of heart,,., hccause the good men of RO many
np:cs past Jrnvc confided it to us to cherish 11nil maintain. We look upon it, as tl1e son
of a long line of worthy fathers looks upon hi" ancestral tower, hullo wed by legends
nutl memories of men in whose veins his own hlootl flowed.
Bnt many times in tlw worl<l's history, p:rcat falHchoods have held the faith of
oarncst men for ages, bearing the banner of Heaven in the front rank of progt-eHa,
wnitc<l upon by dvilization as by a handmaid, accompo.nietl by a visible escort of

Uons find refreshment and repose heneath its sluule, before it ripens ita "<lead sea
fruit of ashes."
We can not say that Masonry will Jive for ever, because it has lived so·lo11g. Nor
clo we find in the mere excellence of its precepts nny sufficient warrant for our belief
ln its perpetnity. We know that its morality is pure, unquestionable. Without tl1ls,
thn moral sense of the world would have scouted and put down the imposture long
ngo. But in this rcgaril there is nothing essentially peculiar in Masonry. Goocl,
wise men, bards and Bages, wrote and taught precepts identically the same, bcfom
tho corner-stone of the Temple was laid. The apostles and pTophets of many a creed
~.hat Jms had its day in tbe worlil fo1· good or evil, and passed into history, have
l.1mght doctrines as pure, a charity as grand and beneficent. We claim no monopoly,
no patent, for the virtues we inculcate. We know, that without this cxocllence, the
lmitltuti-Ou were nothing; and we do not rely upon it as proof conclusive of its endnr·
lll!Ce.
In the negative qualities of Masonry, rather tlmn in any of its positive, apparent
11ttl'ibutes, may be found the assumnce we require. The founders of other systems
or morality llave not been content to regulate the conduct of their followers; they
must control their faith. Not content to shape and guide for the best this life, of

which we may know much, they have sought with keener or duller insight, to penetrate the unfathomable mystery of the life beyond, and have Jinked the intellectual
faith they have devised, indissolubly, to the code of' morals they have inculcated.
Masonry has no creed. It demands nothing from the intellect of its votaries. It
appeals only to the universal heart of man. It demands belief in God as a prerequisite to initiatio.n into its mysteries, a.s it requires free birth and lawful age, because
there can be no perfect manhood worthy of the brotherly Jove we offer, without
belief in a controlling intellect superior to our weak and erring humanity. Ilcyond
this, faith is absolutely free. No brother wears the mantle of his creed across the
portals of the Lodge. It drops from his shoulders when he assumes the Jamb-skin.
No matter by what name he may call upon God elsewhere, no matter through what
forms or ceremonies he may worship Him-in church or synagogue-in mosque or
pagoda-kneeling, humbly, before a shrine niched in cathedral aisles, or erect and
proud beneath the dome of the grander temple not made with hands-within the
sacred precincts of the Lodge are neither Jews nor Christians, worshippers of Brahma,
nor followers of Mahomet ;-only f1·eeme11, brethren, standing in the acknowledgccl
presence of the All-Father.
It deals only with this present, mortal existence; never ignoring a future, grander
one, inculcating not one precept inconsistent with its fullest development, but leaving
its followers free to shape, each by hiA individual conscience, the hopes and fears that
wait upon it. llfore than any other institution of \vhieh we know, it recognize• the
worth of mau, merely as mortal man-the high duties, the privileges, the sorrows of
manhood. It is human in its origin and aims. It bears no commission from Heaven
for the work it has to do. Good men and true, men uninspired save by the spirit of
genuine philanthropy, contrived the scheme for the nse and benefit of man.
Their scheme was simple, befitting the simple age in which it had its origin, yet
evincing not only a broad benevolence but a keen perception of' the wants and capacity of humanity. They saw man as he was, with all the inconsistent elements of
his nature," the suffering, the 1veak, the erring, the wicked, but still the friendly, the
loving child of God, our }'ather." They saw how difficult it was for him to walk
alone in the path of honor and rectitude, amidst the many temptations that surrounded him; and devised a plan of brotherhood and mutual aid. They Raw how
frequently his better impulse• were overcome by his worser passion•, and taught him
to circumscribe his desires, and keep his passions within due bounde. They saw him
exposed to manifold dangers continually, from the malice of enemies and from the
evil of his own heart, and imposed npon his brethren as a solemn dnty, to reach
forth a hand and prevent him from falling, to whisper words of counsel in his ear,
and warn him of all approaching danger. They saw how inevitably sorrow, and
sickness, and death came to him, and so arranged it that his sorrows should be lightened by sympathy and aid, his passage to the grave smoothed and cheered, hiA body
laid reverently within it. More than this; they saw in every free man born into tho
world a flt candidate for the rights and benefits of their broad benevolence, esteeming no man for his worldly wealth or honors, but teaching, in an age of despotism,
that perfect equality of which sages only dared to dream.
.. 'l'hrough all disguise, form, place, or nameBeneath the :flaunting robe of sinThrough poverty and squalld shame,
Tho.y looked upon the man withinOn man, as nian-retaining yet,Howe'er debased, nnd soiled, and dimThe crown upon his forehead setThe Immortal gift of God to him."

And these modest virtues, this grand charity, they taught by precepts so simple,
hy symbols so appropriate, that the humblest intellect could not misapprehend them.
Masonry has Jost nothing in the lapse of ages of the severe simplicity that marked
It• origin. Seated in the hearts of its followers, it leaves the intellect untrammeled,
to Aearch through nature as it will, to resolve as it may all questions of greater import than our well-being here, to monld and fashion at its own pleasure its faith and
hope of the hereafter. It ignore• logic. It will have nothing to do with ultimate
c·.:rnses. It is always monitorial, never argumentative. Tt looks the facts of existMtce full in the face, and dealA with them as actual facts, without any impertinent
whys or wherefores. Sin and selfishneAA exist-grim, ungainly, inexorable faets-no
matter how or why they came into the world. Tell the truth, act upon the square,
nrlmonish, reprove, forgive, and the poison will he neutralized, anil the trail of .the
•erpent will be covered. Sorrow, poverty, disease, came to man-his inalienable bJrth
right. No matter what may be the hidden clesign of Providence in these affiictions,
love, relieve, console, and a blessing will follow the recipient and the giver. It leaves
other systems to arrange as they .ple118e the harmonies of' the nniverse ; its ear i.~
t.urnecl eastward, listening only to the "still, sad music of' humanity." It never
l'P<[uircs it;i followers to belie\'e any thing, only to do something. It JeaveH others t.o
111111 whatever pcarlH of price may be hidden in the dust ancl debris of the dead past;
nncl is content to clistribnte among men, with a free hancl, its own homely treasures,
lt.s corn, wine, anc! oil. Its doctrines were not contrived in cave or cloister-compiled
from faded mam1scripts, the records of worn-out thought-but were read anc\ transt11•rihcd from the plain printed hook of natnre, in the free sun-light and air of heaven,
hr men claimi1w no higher inspiratiou than love ancl good will to man.
· These qualit~s of Masonry that I have endeavored to depict-its genuine philanthropy, its zealous care for the good of man in this present life, and it.s constant
nvoiilance of distrncting Apecnlations concerning the mysteries of another-deter·
mine its proper place among the various systems of benevolence. We do not clai~
for it the highest rank. A system that claims to adjust the relations of man to his
Creator, that puts forth a scheme so comprehensive as to embrace not only life, hut
Immortality, must outrank a, syHtem that only concerns it•elf for the welfare of man
lu this short present existence. Tt is a loftier flight-the effort to solve the great
problems of creation nnd birth, the solemn mystery of death, and the world beyond
t.11e grave. We how with reverence before the intellect that has clared to gmpple
with these mighty themes; and from the small stand point of this brief life, looking
hnf'ore and after, hits set in order the wonderful chaos of' myi;tcry that surrounds it.
We recognize the utility and beauty of all creeds that teach man to use his fragment
of existence here with a view to 11 completer life hereafter. We freely accord to
rnligion a higher place than Masonry, among the agencies of good to man. We claim
for it a lower, broader range, one broad as humanity. We claim for it the highest
place among those systems of benevolence devised by man, unaided by a higher
power, for the benefit of mortal life alone. It iA a pure, simple, efficient plan of good,
II' not administering to man's loftiest desires, never pandering to his baser passions.
It iA the table land ;-stretching broad and fair beneath the eye of Heaven; glisten·
Ing with harvests, clotted with roofs; the smoke from countless pe:iceful fire sides
floating over its broad rivers hearing its abundance to the sea; the living-toiling,
rcJoicing, and sorrowing, upon its surface-the dead, resting quietly within its bosom.
l•'tir below are the marshes and fens, luxuriant with rank and noisome vegetation, the
nhocle of loathsome reptile•, breeding fevers and death; far above, are the glittering
uwuntain peaks,-magnificcot, cold, cheerle.ss-the awful Sinai tops, whither the
prophets go up to commune with God and receive his Jaw. The inundation that
r11vages the low lands, spares its harvests; the storm that sweeps the mount(liD, an<l
lllQ~ens the avitlanche, passes it over, unharmed.

In the essential humanity of Masonry, in its careful separation from all forms of
religious faith, lies the secret of its. universality, the logical proof of its perpetuity.
These qualities have preser\'ed it for us-will preserve it for those who :trc to come
after us. Creeds die, man lives. Creeds appeal to the intellect of man. Whatever
belongs to the intellect, must be affected by its inevitable Jaw of growth. The man of
the nineteenth century can not receive with absolute, unquestioning faith the belief
of one or two thousand yem·s ago. You cun not clothe a giant with the garment of a
pigmy. They are but steps in
"'J'hc grcr1..t world's altar stairs
That s101rn 1 through darkness,. up to God; H

standing fast, while the race mounts over am] pa.st them in its onward march. All
along the path over which man has trnvelerl since the birth of time, arc scattered
the rnins of forsaken creeds, dead watch tires, serving now only to mark the spots
where the army of civilization once camped for a night.
X o fear that brotherly lo»c, relief, and trutl1, ;vill lose their virtue by the lapse of
time. No hope that the conditions of mortal lifo will ever be 80 changed that pov·
crty, sorrow, sickness, death, will not call for sympathy and aid; that passion and
prejudice will uot nccfl tltc friendly cheek, the kind reproof; tlutt error and sin will
not require that generous cbarit,y, that" sn!fcretlt long and is kinu!' The intellect
can ncver reae 11 a height so cold and chee1·less tlmt the warmth of social fellowship
will be unfelt, uncared for; that it will not be a heartfelt IJ!casurc to detect a brother
by tl1c subtle instinct of the Craft., whcrn tho eye sees only a stranger.
We hope that Masonry will live, because we know its aims arc gooil, and pure,
and generous. We know that it will live, because it has never invoked the dangerous
aid of intellect, the waxen wings of learns, that have borne many a worthy institn·
tion to a loftier, only to sink it to a lower, thuu its hnmhlc place; and because it
deals only with those clements of man's nature that can not forsake him while he retains his humanity-that arc of' the very woof and warp of manhood. Through tl1e
long ages that are coming, as in the centuries through which it has come down to us,
we see our beloved institution pursning the even tenor of its humble life-. its puro
precepts passing from lip to lip of good men and true_:its symbols, mute, yet elo·
qncnt, teaching tlieir accnstomed lcASous of charity antl goo cl will to man-its worthy
deeds umvitncssed-its peaceful triumphs nnsung-drnpping its manifold blessings,
noislessly, unheralded, as Heaven tlrops its dew. Anil who knows, but when He
sha.11 make np his reconl of those works of human lrnnds that have served Him best
in time, He will give a higher place than we ha\'e claimed for it to an institution that
has never souglit to part nnd peer behiud the rnil which He has seen fit to throw
about His providence - that has cared, not so mnch for the glory of Him, the Cre·
ator, as"for the good of His humble creature-and Masonry be accepted, not only of
man, the brother, but of God, the beneficent Fatbcr.

choice which you have made.
We are now about to separate, each to go to his own home,-to !he i'C(me nf the
active duties of life. In the disc barge of those unties, us Masons, let us strive to Jive up
to the line of duty marked out by our obligations and the precepts of our Order; let ns

widow and the Ol'Jlhan; and, whilst as loyal citizens we stand by the constituted an·
thorities of the laud, let us do all that lies in our power to promote " peace on earth
and good will amongst men." Let us be distinguished, as fathers, husl>ands, broth·
crs, and sons, for the practice of all those domestic virtues which renuer home happy
and give a charm to life ; and in all our relations let us endeavor to deserve the appellation of' good citizens and good men ; so that, having finisheil our course here
below-and the day of the departure of all of us from this sublunary spl1ero is not far

SECTION 1. The Grand Master, Deputy Grand Master, Grand Wardens, Grand

SEC. 2. All other Grand Officers shall be appointed by the Grand Mn.ster, immediately after his installation, at ea.ch Annual Communication ; shall !Jc properly
invested before the close thereof; and shall hold their re"yiective offices dnring his
will and pleasure.

preceding the date of his application. Nor shall any Lodge receive such application
from any person, who, within twelve months next preceding, shall have been rejected
by any Lodge, unless by dispensation from the Grand Master, as provided in Sec. 1,
Art. I, Part IL All such applications, as well as those for affiliation, shall be in writing, signed by the applicant, and recommended by at least two members of the
Lodge, in the forms prescribed in Art. III, Part VII.
SEC. 3. No Lodge shall ballot upon such application, (except by dispensation
from the Grand Master, as provided in Sec. 1, Art. I, Part II,) until it shall have been
referred to a committee, whose duty it shall be to make strict examination into the
moral, mental, and physical qualifications of the applicant, and to report thereon at
the next stated meeting, unless further time be granted. No application shall be
withdrawn after reference to a committee, and it shall require an unanimous ballot
to elect. But if one black ball, only, appear in the ballot-box, the Master, without
declaring the result, may at once order a second ballot for the purpose of correcting
a possible mistake.
SEC. 4. No dispensation shall be issued to a Lodge to ballot for and confer the
degrees upon a candidate, without reference to a committee as provided i.u the preceding section, nor to receive and act upon the petition of a rejected applicant within
less than twelve months after the date of such rejection, unless the application therefor be made by the Lodge, by a unanimous vote; and of the special meeting to be
holden under such dispensation, and the purpose thereof, the members of the Lodge
shall have due notice.
SEc. 5. No Lodge, unless it be otherwise provided in its by-laws, slrnll have
more than one ballot for the three degrees; but, though an applicant may be elected
to receive them, if, at any time before his initiation, objection be made by any mcm-'
ber, he shall not receive the degree until such objection shall have been withdrawn:
and if, after his initiation, but before being passed, on after passing, before being
raised, objection to his advancement be made by any member, such objection shall
be referred to a committee, with power to inquire into the cause thereof, who shall
at the next stated meeting (unless further time be given,) report thereon; and upon
the reception of such report, if no cause for the objection has been assigned, or if
the cause assigned be, in the opinion of two-thirds of the members present, not a
valid and Masonic one, the Lodge may confer the degree in the same manner as if no
objection had been made.
SEc. 6. No Lodge shall advance an Entered Apprentice or a Fellow Craft to 11
higher degree until, after a strict examination in open Lodge, he shall have given
811tisfactory evidence that he is entirely proficient and well qualified in that or those
which he has already taken ; and no Entered Apprentice or Fellow Craft shall be •
advanced to a higher degree in any Lodge other than that in which he shall have
received those, or either of those degrees, unless by the official consent of such
Lodge, if it then be in ex~stencc.
SEc. 7. No Lodge within this State shall confer the three degrees for a less fee
than fifty dollars, nor shall nny Lodge without the State, and under this jurisdiction,
confer them for a less fee than thirty dollars ; and in every case the fee for each, or
all of the degrees, as may be regulated by the Lodge, sh11ll accompany the application.

SEC. 7. After all the testimony shall have been receive<!, the CommisRioncrs shall

SEC. 8. The penalties which may be inflicted are repriman<l in open Lodge, sus·

the Grand Secretary, together with information of the appeal intended, if any there be.
ARTICLE V.
OF REVISIONS AND RESTORATIONS.
SECTION 1. All judgments from which an appeal shall be taken as hereinbefore
in this Part provided, shall be reviewed in the Grand Lodge, or before a committee
thereof, during its sessions, upon the record sent up, and upon such other proper
uocuments as may be submitted ; and its decision shall be final an<! conclusive.
SEC. 2. All sentences of suspension shall be for an indefinite perio<l ; an<! a Lodge
may, at any state<! meeting, by the votes of two-thirds of the members present, annul
any such sentence of suspension pronounced by itself, and restore the Mason thus
suspended to all his Masonic rights; Provided, that notice of a resolution for such
restoration shall have been given at the stated meeting next preceding. And in case
of sueh restoration, the Secretary shall at once notify the Grand Secretary thereof.

REPRESENTATIVE.-The representative of a Lodge within this State, is one who, be·

VACANCY.-Vacancies in office, either in a Lodge or in the Grand Lodge, may occur
by death, deprivation, resignation, removal from the jurisdiction, suspension, or expulsion.
JuRISDici•roN.-The jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge includes all Lodges and Masons within the territorial limits of this State, and all Lodges and their members without this State, acting under its authority:
The jurisdiction of a Lodge includes all ~!asons residing nearer to its place of
meeting than to that of any other Lodge within this State, except in towns or cities
where more than one Lodge exists ; in which case, each of such Lodges ,has sepa·
rate jurisdiction over its own members, and concurrent jurisdiction over all Masons
not members of one of such Lodges, who reside in such town or city, or nearer thereto than to any other place where a Lodge exists.
REGULATION. - By a regulation of the Grand Lodge is mel\nt any resolution, edict,
law, or ordinance of any kind whatever, other than the Constitution, which it may
adopt.
SuSPENSION.-The suspension of a Lodge iH an arrest of its charter, and a tempora1·y prohibition to as8emble or work as a leg«! Lodge, until again authorized so to
do by competent authority ; and the act Ruspends all its members except those especially exempted from its effect.
The suspension of the Master of a Lodge is a temporary deprivation of his office,
and prohibits all recognition of him in that capacity, until he he restored by compe·
tent authority.
The suspension of a Mason is a temporary deprivation of' all his rights and privileges us such, aml prol1ibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse whatever with him, until he shall be legally restored by the Lodge which suspended him, or by the Grand Lodge.
Exri:LS!ON.--The expulsion of a :1.Iason is tlte highest penalty known to the Masonic Jaw. It is an absolute deprivation of all the rigl1ts and privileges of the Order,
and prohibits all Masons and Lodges from holding any Masonic intercourse with him
forever, unless he he restored by the Grand Lodgl'NorIPICATION. -A notification is t\ call issuetl by the Secretary, by order of tlrn
Lodge or Master, or by other competent authority as hereinbefore provided, to nt·
tenrl for some specific purpose at the time and place therein indicated ; and it is the
duty of ernry llason to comply with its direction, if he can, without grent inconven·
ience, do so.
SUMMONs.-A summons is an imperative order, issued by the Master, or by otl1er
competent authority a8 hereinbefore provided, to appear at such time and place as
may therein be designated. The obligation to obey it is absolute, and the penalty
for disobedience shall be expulsion, unless it shall be shown that such disobedience
was unavoidable, or was occasioned by some pressing necessity.
STATED MEETlNGS. - The statetl meeting of a Lodge is the one only meeting in
each lunar month, at which business may be done, with the exceptions specified in
Sec. 2, Art. II, Part III. It shall be designated as such in the by-laws of each Lodge,
aml no adjourned or called meeting shall ever be considerer! ns a part of such stated
meeting.

The Senior Grand Warden then poured the wine upon the stone, saying:"May the Great Giver of all good enable the craftsmen in due time to complete
tbis stately edifice; and, during their intervals from labor, may they constantly be
blessed with that refreshment of which this Wine is emblematical."

The Junior Grand Warden next poured the oil upon the stone, saying:
"May the blessing of Heaven descend upon this and all good works; and may
our loved Fraternity long exist to pour forth the Oil of joy upon the hearts of the
widowed, the fatherless, and the distressed."

'rhe Grand Master then said:·"May the All-Bounteous Author of Creation lend aid to those who have conceived
imd thus far carried on this goodly enterprise ; may He protect the workmen em·
ployed upon this building from every accident, and long preserve it for the important
uses which it is destined to subserve; may He grant to us all an ever-bountiful 'supply
of the Corn of Nourishment, the Wine of Refreshment, and the Oil of Joy ; may those
who shall hereafter congregate within its halls remembertl1eir oa.ths and their duties to
their God, to their fellow-men, and to themselves; and may the blessing of'Heaven
rest upon all our Craft, and upon all the people of these United States." ·

"Brother Principal Architect : Helying upon your skill in our noble art, I now
corrfide to you these implements of Operative Masonry. May this undertaking be
speedily accomplished; may there be no envy, discord, or confusion among the
workmen ; may you perform the important duties with which you have been charged,
not only to the satisfaction of those who have entrusted you with their fulfillment,
but in such manner as shall secure the approbation of your own conscience, and re·
dound to the honor of our Ancient Crnft; and when this, and all our work on earth
io done, may we all be permitted to assemble in that glorious Grand Lodge above,
where the Supreme Architect of the Universe himself presides."

'fhe Grand Master and his officers then returned to the platform, the
band playing " Hail to the Chief," and the Grand Marshal, by direction,

"The craftsmen having faithfully and skillfully performed their duty, I now declare
the foundation stone of this Capitol building to be well formed, true and trusty. May
it long remain, and may the building which is to be erected upon it exist for ages aa
an evidence of the prosperity, the happiness, and the patriotism of a free, happy, and
Independent people."

By order of the Most Worshipful Grand Master of Masons in California, and in
the name of the Grand Lodge thereof, I now proclaim the corner·stone of this public
edifice to be laid in due a.nd ample form, according to the ancient usages and customs
of Free and Accepted Masons.

The petitions for the foregoing dispensations, with the <limits of the several petitioners, the recommendations of the neighboring chartered Lodges, the certificates as
to the qualifications of the officers proposed, and the other papers required by our
laws, were all in proper form and are herewith presented, together with sundry letters relative thereunto.
Another vacancy has occurred in the numbers borne upon our registry. Early in
June last, information was received from Bro. GEORGEH. CoE, the Master of' Oi·o Fino
Lodge, N o.137, at Oro Fino, in Siskiyou county, of the total destruction, by fire, of the
hall of that body, together with its charter, records, and property of' every description; and, after certain correspondence relative to the proper manner of' carrying
into effect the desire of its members that the Lodge be dissolved in consequence
thereof, and of the fact that the greater portion of its members had removed from the
neighborhood, on the eighteenth <lay of October last a formal surrender of its rights
nuder the charter granted in 1860 was transmitted to this office. It will be seen from
the correspondence relative to this surrender, herewith submitted, that the liabilities
of that Lodge have all been satisfied by the voluntary contributions of its members;

111111 it is but just to say that, during its brief existence, few Lodges in the State were
ht•tl.or conducted than that of' our unfortunate brethren at Oro Fino. Its dues were
pnid in full, and its returns, to the <late of surrender, have been furnished by its late
MnHtcr, as complete as was possible under the circumstances.
111 addition to the foregoing, another Lodge has, for the present, at least, ceased
II" labors. ln August last, certain complaints which had reached this office relative
111 nllege<l great irregularities in Unity Lodge, No. 130, at San Bernardino, were

l'lllJIOWering him to make an examination of the manner in which the affairs of that
I.11tlge were administered, and of the character and proceedings of its officers anil
lll!'lllbers; and directing him to report such facts as he should ascertain, together with
""''" opinions in regartl to the proper course to lie pursued in respect to that body,
llH his inquiries and information should justly prompt. The manner in which Bro.
l.ANJJIOR has discharged the unpleasant duty thus assigned him, has atforde<l ample
proof that the confidence of the Grand Master was well bestowed. He proceeded at
11111·e to San Bernardino-a distance of more than a hundred miles, and by a not very
1•11mf'ortable means of conveyance-where he foithtnlly ancl thoroughly carried his
Instructions into ellect; and, on the third tlay of' October last, he transmitted a report
111 the Grand Master, so full and complete, as to the information elicited, and so con·
ri11cing, as to the conclusions deduced therefrom, that that officer at once directed
th" anest of the charter of the offending Lodge. An order to that ctlect was trans111itte<l to Bro. H. C. HussELL, its Master, on the twenty-second <lay of October last,

The Grand Secretary presented his Annual Report, as follows:To the M.·. W.·.Grand Lodge of Califomia :In obedience to that portion of the Constitution which prescribes the duties of the
Grand Secretary, the undersigned again presents a report of such transactions of his
office during the past year as requires action on the part of the Grand Lodge, or as
may be of interest to it, simply as matter of information.
As soon as practicable after the close of the last Annual Communication, the
usual number of copies of the proceedings thereat were printed and distributed
among the Lodges, or reserved for binding, sale, and use at the present meeting, as
has heretofore been customary. The publications of the other Grand Lodges;with
which we are in correspondence, have not come to hand as promptly during the past
year as it has hitherto been our good fortune to be enabled to chronicle ; and the
undersigned has to express his regret that, for the year 1861, no proceedings have
been received from Alabama, Arkansas, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Florida,
Georgia, Iowa, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nebraska, New York, North
Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, and Washington Territory; while
from South Carolina nothing has reached him since 185U, and from Ohio nothing since
1858. The unhappy attitude which has been assumed by a portion of the States above
named towards the Government of the United States, will of cou1'8e account for a
portion of these failures; and for the remainder, the writer can only hope that the
deficiencies will be supplied when this shall attract the notice of the several Grand
Secretaries.

The Committee on Jurisprudence decided: "That when a member of a subordinate Lodge is suspended for non-payment of dues, he cannot be reinstated until all
dnes to the Lodge of which he is a member, both those which accrued up to the time
of his suspension, and subsequently to the time of his reinstatement, are paid "-a
decision which corresponds with the law of our own jurisdiction. 1'here were three
cases before the committee. The second was whether a member of one Lodge can
prefer charges for unmasonic conduct against a member of another, or whether the
eharges shonlrl be made by the Lodge of which the complainant is a member. We
think the committee decided rightly: "That a ]\faster Mason in one Lodge has a right
to prefer charges for unmasonic conduct against a mt mber of another Lodge, and such
charge shouhl be investigated and, if sustained, punished.'' If Masons will be guilty
of grossly violating our laws and regulations, they should be dealt with, no matter
from what source the information is first obtained. The third case is presented in
this wise: "A Past Master of a Lodge is in the habit of freely and publicly denouncing the Holy Writings as untrue, unworthy of respect, and not to be believed. What,
if any, should be his punishment?" The committee answer: "His conduct is grossly
nnmasonic, and should subject him to expulsion." 'l'he decisions of the committee
were all approved by the ()rand I odge. We are pleased to see that the Committee
on Jurisprudence was made one of the standing committees.

wise: "When Roger Williams fled from persecution in Massachusetts, as he crossed

Since writing the above, we have learned, with great sorrow, of the death of
Grand Master TUCKER, at his home in Vergennes, in the month of April, 1861. In his
life he was pure; in his death he was happy- reacly to welcome the grim messenger
as a kind friend. To our brethren of Vermont the loss is irreparable-the last of
their Grand Masters is gone - and we most sincerely condole with them in their bereavement. A good man, a trne friend, a zealous Mason, an earnest, sincere Chris·
tian, full of honors, full of years, loved and respected by all who knew him, he has
gone to his rest-gone to receive the rewards that await the faithful in that realm
where light and life eternal reign forever. From 1824 to the ela,y of his eleath he was
an officer of the Grand Lodge of Vermont-in 1824 and 1825 Junior Grauel Deacon;
in 1826, Senior Grand Deacon; in 1827 and 1828, Junior Grand Warelen; from 1829 to
1846, Deputy Grancl Master, and from 1817 to 1861, Grand Muster. Bro. HOLLENBECK,
the present venerable Grand Secretary, was first electeel to that office in 1883, and for
nearly thirty years, he has continued to fill most 11cceptably that honorable position.
May his lamp of life yet long hold out to burn.

Bro. H. L. PALMER, Past Grand Master, presented the Report on Correspondence,
a well written summary of the proceedings of twenty-six Grand Lodges, our own
among the nnmber. The Grand Lecturer, Bro. M. L. You:-1os, reports the Lodges
"in a more prosperous condition than ever before. adding to their numbers full as
many as in preceding years, and generally of the best material. They are paying
more than ordinary attention to the workings of the Lodge, endeavoring to be correct
and precise in the ritual of the three degrees, so 1hat we are getting each year a more
perfect uniformity of work among the different Lodges throughout our jurisdiction."
Bro. RoB. Moaars, Past Grand Master of Kentncky, was there and was invited to
favor the Grand Lodge with a lecture, which he did. Later in the session the Grand
Lectnrer was requested "to exemplify the work of our Grand Ludge," which leaves
an impression that the brethren there did not altogether agree to and adopt Bro. MoRms' Prcston·Wcbh system. Applicat on was made by the officers of the Third Regiment for a dispensation to form a military Lodge. The committee, to whom it was
referred, reported it" inexpedient to take any action thereon at present." A resolution was introduced, providing for the publication of' the proceedings of the Grand
Lodge from its organization, which was referred to a committee, who are to report
n.t the ucxt Communication. That is a step in the right direction, and we hope ere
long to see a full reprint of the proceedings of all our Grand Lodges. A resolution
was also introduced to pay the committees on finance, returns, and credentials,
which was very properly rejected. If committees can not do their dnty without pay,
they had better drop out and give place to those who have a heart in the work. It
is fitting and proper that the necessary expenses of representatives should be paid,
either by the Lodges that SPlld them, or by the Grand Lodge out of a common fund;
but we do not like the notion, which seems to be gaining ground, that nobody can
do anything unless he is paid in the current coin of the realm-that representatives
must be paid by the day-that committees must be paid-and every body paid.
The financial affairs of the Grand Lodge seem to be in excellent condition. The
report of the Grand Treasurer shows $11,173 on hand-the receipts for the year
$2850, and the disbursements $1727; and from the proceedings before us we judge
the fraternity in Wisconsin to be in a most prosperous and healthy condition in all
respects. Five new Lodges were established during the year, under dispcusations,
making the number of the Lodges one hundred and nineteen; and the membership
is reported at 3757. The proceedings arc very neatly printed, and are gotten up
altogether in a very superior style.
The Ill.'. W.'. AI.YIN B. ALDEN was elected Grand Master, and the R.'. W.'. WILLIAM 'l'. PALMER was elected Grand Secretary.

extra volume that might he cut, and on which one might make marginal noteR and
references without offonse to anybody.
All which is respectfully submitted.

If there ls a feature more prominent arnl clear than another in the discussion of
this subject, it is the persistent, tenacious, and strong grasp with which the Grand
Lodge of Maine holds on to the question-" Has a subordinate of one Grand Lodge
the right to make Masons of persons residing within the jurisdiction of another Grand
Lodge, without its consent?" It set out with the principle, because the discussion
arose under the heavy pressure of a grievance; and they are seeking to maintain it
in order to preserve harmonious intercourse between their frontier Lodges, and those
of their British American brethren. We fail to discover anything in all the records
we have had access to, whereby the Grand Lodge of Maine can be justly charged
with '·claiming the right of following a man, merely because he once U1!ed within a
ilistrict, when he had removed to another place;" bat, on the contrary, it appears to
us that that body only claims the right for its subordinates to exercise exclusive
jurisdiction over resident material, and that this jurisdictional right follows that
moveable jewel only so long as it claims its residence, and leaves its tent and hahita·
tion behind, within her borders. The. wise policy of this law seems plain to us, we
believing that our noble Order, even with its many safeguards, ha.s yet too few to
protect it to justify us in relaxing, in the slightest degree, a single one, however
unessential it may appear in its use. We say law, because we have been under the
impression that the principle was stamped with the character of universality, and
needed only that other essential element, antiquity, to raise it almost to the dignity
of a landmark. It is based UjlOn the wholesome idea that, inasmuch as Freemasonrv
is intended to select the well-tried, true, and trusty men of the world to clothe
her honors, the knowledge of the "real wortlt and personal merit" should be derived
always from those who have, by the nature of' circumstances, the best opportunity of
knowing whether those who seek admittanct' to our temples are endowed with the
necessary qualifications.

British Provinces on this continent to respect this Masonic usage of our country, so
neeessary for our good government and harmony.

A subordinate Lodge, for the safety of' our institution, should he the ROie judge, as
it certainly is the best, whether the resident within its jnrisdiction who knocks at the
door of Free :Masonry is " a good man and true, free horn, of mature and discreet
age, no bondman, no woman, no immoral and Rcan(Jalous man, but of good report;"
and if the Bohemian doctrine is admitted, that every Lodge may exercise the
abstract right to initiate any person whom it may cousider fit and proper, without
considering where his residence may be, we reverse the practice in the Lodges of
the American States and yield a principle which, in its practice, has been productive
of the most visible and palpable good.
