Yonr committee, to whom was reforrc<l the following <p1e><tion, i•rnposed by Bro .
•Jons R. IlucKnr:ti, to wit: " lfo~ n. subordinate Lodge the right, under Hee. O, Art..
III, Part III, of the Constitution, to reHtorc" llfason laboring 11rnlcr suspension for
non-payment of !lueA, in any other manner than that provitled for in the fundamental
law - that iH, by 1iayiug all arreara1rns due- in other wordH can a J,oill(c remit •hw'
until a brother is reHtorcd ?" beg leave to report a,; follows:Tile proposition is s1rnccptibk of clivMon into two brunche• ~the riucstion of
obedience to laws, nnd the question of construction of laws. Jn answer to the first,
it is the opinion of the committee that a subordinate Louge can do nothing rightfully,
•1ither in respect to the restoration of a l\fason laboring under snspension for nonpayment of dues, or any other matter, in any way other than that provided in the
fundamental law. In answer to the second, it is the opinion of the committee that
the fnndamental laws of Masonry respecting its morality shoultl be construed strictly,

[115]

356

[May 15,

Proceedings of the

but always with charity; in respect to its government, with liberality, and in the true
spirit of the enactments and customs. To say that a Lodge !lannot remit a portion
or all of the arrearngea, for good and satisfactory reasons, of a member suspended
for non-payment of dues, lu order that be may be restored, appears to us like the
construction which Shylock would have put upon hfa bond. We do not believe that
such a spirit did, or could exist in the Masonic mind of the framers of our funda·
mental law; and we are therefore of the opinion that a subordinate Lodge, for good
cause, in the exercise of a discreet judgment, under the section referred to, may
remit dues in favor of a member suspended for non-payment of dues, in order to
restore him.
All which is respectfully submitted.

Your committee desire here, in the most solemn manner, to express anew their
abhorrence of the practice of' dueling at any and all times, hut more especially he·
tween Masons. They cannot, however, Le liliud to the fact that, ordinarily, and
perhaps always, the Llame of omission attaches as strongly to the Lodge within
whose jurisdiction a duel occurs, as does the offence of c6mmission attach to the
offending brethren. They cannot conceive of a difficulty between Masons that may
not readily Le settled by the Lodge itself - if need be - acting in its capacity as a
Lodge, thereLy preventing an appeal to arms. They most earnestly recommend
should a similar cause of difference arise hereafter between Lrethren, that the Maste~
of the Lodge within whose jurisdiction they may he, immediately proceed himself to
settle the difference existing, if in his power; and, if' he fail in this, that he forthwith
summon the offending brethren arnl the members of his Lodge to take action upon
it: for surely a little time and trouble is well consumed if thereby we may prevent a
breach of not on,ly our own laws, Lut the laws of' the land, and perchance save the
shedding of fraternal blood.

action of the erring brethren. 'l'he Lodges to which they severally belonged, and

'l'he proposition of Bro. JOHN W. HARVILLE, to amend Sec. I, Art. IV, Part I, is in
effect to change the time of the Annual Communications of the Grand Lodge to the
second Tuesday of August. This is a question of convenience for the Grand Lodge
to decide, and is reported back to it without comment.
'l'he proposition of Bro. JOSHUAH. VARIEL, to amend Sec. 2, Art. IV, Part VI, is
in effect to change the present mode of constituting a commission to try offences, by
maldng it the duty of the Master to appoint the commissioners, in lieu of the present
troublesome and unsatisfactory process of election by the Lodge. It is believed that
the change will he in every 'my beneficial, and it is recommended that the proposal
be udopted.

for its object the concealment of the name of a brother who prefers charges against
>tnother for unmasonic conduct. Your committee think that a Mason may at least be
suspected of 11 lack of moral courage who will care for the benefit which such an
amendment would give him, and they recommend that it be not adopted.
'l'he other proposition of Bro. J08IAH g. S'rEVENs, to amend Sec. I, Art. V, Part

Your committee, to whom was referred a memorial from certain members of'
lloldRn aate Lodge, No. 30, located in the city of San Francisco, have carefully
and attentively considered the questions thereiu raised, and beg leave to report as
follows:It is represented that at the stated meeting of the said Lodge, held on the evening
of the third day of December, 1861, it elected its officers for the then ensuing Masonic
year. One hundred and three members were present. The officers were regularly
ballotetl for, and Bro. LAWRENm; C. Owu:N, a member, having received fifty-two votes
for the office of Master, that being a majority of all the Yotes of the members present,
was declared by the Muster then presiding to be elected to the said office for the ensn·
ing Masonic year. A number of brethren now remonstrate against his holding the
office, upon the ground that he was illegally elected.
We believe that this is the first case of a contested election occurring in our juris·
diction. The brethren remonstrating declare that one Mason, who was present and
voted, was an illegal voter, and this being so, that Bro. OWEN did not receive a majority of the votes of the members present, as required by the Constitution, and con·
sequently his election is void. They charge that a brother named JonN VALENTIN};,
a, so-called honorary member, was an illegal voter, and that he is the Mason to whom
they refer.
The interesting question-which has, as we believe, never been decided by our
Grand Lodge -what is an honorary member, and what are his privileges? is here
raised. Membership in a Lodge, as declared in our present Constitution, may be
acquired in three ways; by having regularly received the degree of Master Mason
therein ; by being duly elected for affiliation therewith; or by having been named
in a <lispensation for a new Lodge as one of the petitioners therefor. There can be
no tlonbt in our jurisdiction as to the mode of acquiring membership at the present
time. •
Honorary membership, Bro. MACK};y declares, is quite a recent invention, and is
now conferred only as a mark of distinction. We learn that our own WASHINGTON,
and, during his revisit to our country nearly forty years ago, our brother the Marquis
de LAPAYETTE, had this honor conferred upon them. Jn later days, Bro. Lu:BI"ANC EE
MAil<;ONNAY, of ~'ranee, was honored by the Grand Lodge of Massachusetts with the
rank of' 8enior Grand Warden; Bro. Pmur C. TUCKER, of Vermont, was honored
by the Grand Lodge 'of Canada with the rank of Past Grand Master; and Bro. HOBERT
MonRis, of Kentucky, at the same time, by the same body, with the rank of Deputy
tlrnnd Master; and we cite these instanceA to show that honorary membership is not
without distinguished precedents in America. The Grand Lodge of Virginia defines
an lrnnorary member to mean one who is entitled to all the privileges and honors
conferred by Lodge membership, while he is exempt from all the requirements of
such Louge, as set forth in its by-laws; be pays no dues, attends no summonses,
except voluntarily, etc. After this definition, it expresses, by resolution, its disap·
prov~\ of the practice, when such election exempts a brother from all or any of the
rcqm~·ements of Masonry ; and declares that it should not be conferred, except in
eertam cases, and then only upon a poor and meritorious brother- as for instance
upon a Past Master who is unable to pay dues in two Lodges, and whose services ar:
needed in forming a new Lodge ; on old members of dormant Lodges whose names
are necessary, after their affiliation with other Lodges, for the purpose of reviving

Bro. GILBERT B. CLAIBORNE, from the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports : -

376

Proceedings of the

[May 17,

the dormant one; and on Masons called uy duty to be absent in another country.
Tbe whole of tbe legislation of the Grand Lodge of Virginia upon this subject seems
simply to tend toward charity-- the lightening of the burden of Masonry whenever
it bears heavily upon the shoulders of an unfortunate brother who is too modest and
sensitive to admit his inability, either in means or in physical capacity, to contribute
as he would wish to the good of the order.
The committee on Correspondence of the Grand Lodge of Alabama speak of it
as a new kind of memben;bip, pronounce it an anomaly in Masonry, and declare it to
be unsanctioned by the history of the order, by its ancient rules and regulations, or
by healthy modern practice.
These are tbe opinions and decisions of those other jurisdictions who have spoken
most freely on the question. Let us see how far the Grand Lodge of California has
gone over the same way. Our committee on Corresponuence ulluuc to this subject
in their report for 1855, and in referring to the Virginia decision, speak of it only in
the sense in which honorary membership confers worldly honor-that is-in the
Masonic worlu. Their opinion is given in connection with the cases of Bros. LAFAYETTE
and DE MAR90NNA y, and they say that the conferring of this honor shoulu not exempt
the recipient from his proper contributions to the Masonic craft, if his ability will permit him to present them, nor excnse him from any of the requirements of Masonry.
That committee, in presenting this upon the "ubject, in connection with the names of
the distinguished brethren upon whom this membership was conferred as an honorary
rank, advance just the opinion which will apply to the custom >vhen practiced as an
honorary benefit; and with the committee we sec no reason to ditl'er. If a worthy
brother is made an honorary member on account of his misfortunes, as in the case
presented by the Virginia committee- a brother who when in health and prosperity
attenued its meetings punctually, contributed to its charities, and provided for the
wants of needy brethren-we feel very sure that when prosperity again shines upon
his pathway, he will renew his old habits, his ability only having been held in abeyance, but not his will.
We go further than our committee on Conesponuence, whose opinions we have been
considering, in expressing our own opinion on the subject, only so far as concerns
our own jurisdiction. A subordinate Lodge may, for goou reasons of its own, release
a member from the requirements which impose upon him active duties and relieve him
from contributions -say for such reasons as the Virginia committee give; bljt it can
not relieve itself from its own responsibility, assumed in bearing his name upon the
roll. The Lodge thus expressing towaru a cherished brother-its member-the
estimation in which he is held, may call that act by any name it. may select, whether
honorary or not, but your committee certainly think there is nothing,in this jurisdic·
tion which justifies such a Masonic title, and we do not know outside of it where the
custom legitimately originated, nor do we approve of it.
But the qnestion to be decided, and of most importance to the brethren of Golden
Gate Lodge is whether Bro. JouN VALENTINE, who voted at the election for officers
in saiu Lodge, at its stated meeting iu December last, was a member at that time.
We have already saiu how membership is to be acquired under our present Constitution-by strict compliance with that fundamental Jaw and the by-laws of the subordinate Lodges, approved by the Grand Louge if in communication, otherwise by the
Grand Master. 'l'he brethren who sign the papers presented to us in remonstrance,
aver their belief that Bro. V AI,t:NTINE cast his vote for Bro. OWEN at the election
mentioned. They aver also that Bro. VALENTINE !lid not obtain his membership as
required by the present Constitution, and that he hall never signed the by-laws as is
required by the uniform couc auopted by Golden Gate Lodge, anu then in force; all
of which Bro. OWEN admits.
There is proof to show that the Lodge has heretofore always consiuereu him a.
member; that all the brethren, including those who now complain, have not only ~"

[ 136]

1862.J

Grand Lodge of California.

377

tolerated but acted with him ; and that he has ever exercised all the rights of membership, which it seems have never been questioned, until the election of Bro. OWEN.
His name was returned in the annual reports to the Grand Lodge for several years
prior to the occurrence which now brings his name before us, as member and honorary member so called; and unes were annually paid to the Grand Lodge for him.
This shows good faith at least, in every point. lt is further in proof that the brother
was considereu a member, acted us such, anu exerciseu all the rights and discharged
all the duties of a regular member, except in so far as the Lodge chose to release
him, as a so calleu honorary member, long before anu at the time of the adoption of
the present Constitution. The auoption of that Constitution depriveu no Mason of a
right which he was before enjoying, but it enumerated the duties of officerli and
members more clearly, ani! provided more definitely for that which should occur in
the future.
The charge that the brother has not signed the by-laws is one that ought not to be
maue in a well governed Lodge now. If he has not done so, he has certainly neglected his duty, but that neglect can not forfeit his membership, any more than
would the neglect or violation of any other provision which they contain, until after
due trial for such offence, that penalty should be incurred ; and this fact shows that
the officers have been careless in the discharge of their duty, anu that the brethren
themselves cannot avoid a share of the blame which attaches in this case. We advise
the Masters of Lodges who have not attenued to this plain duty, to look well to it.
The opinion of the committee is that Bro.VALENTINE was a member of Golden
Gate Lodge, No. 30, at the time of the election of officers held on the 3d day of
December, 1861; that his vote was legal; and that Bro. LAWRENCE C. OWEN was lawfully elected Master of the said Lodge at that time.
All which is respectfully submitted.

The W.-. HUMPHREY GRIFFI'l'H, Grand Orator, delivoreJ the Annual
Address before the Grand Lodge, as followR : 'l'o 'fHE

M.·. lV>. GRAND MASTEll
AND BRETrrm;N OF THE GRAND LODGE:-

Again, mindful of the duty we owe to our ancient and honornble order, we have
tLssembled to deliberate and act for the good of the craft; and, having discharged
the weightier duties that called us together, we pause from our labors to look back
through the past, that we may thereby gain wisdom and strength for the future.

[146]

1862.J

Grand Lodge of California.

387

Well and proper is it that we should do so, for to our hands, in part at least, is committed f.he prosperity, the usefulness, and the honor of our association.
Par back in the past, where the moRs of centuries clusterR thick upon the pages
of history, Masonry was. lts temples and its columns were reared, its principles
taught, and its name revered, before even HiHtory itself was; the' dim light of tradi·
tion alone can tell us its origin. Not only ancient but honorable has been its name.
It comes clad in the venerable garmentA of departed centuries, ancl crowned with
the favor and countenance of the wise and good who have gone before us; its greatness in no place stained with cruelty or blood; its traditions so pure and S') truthful
that neither the most ardent or the most scrupulous of its votaries cuu wish for their
change ; its honors to be read in enduring monuments of wisdom anti science, of
industry and skill, and in the mouldering and stupendous ruins of the mighty works
wrought by those ancient Masons who were both operative and speculative ; ite
moral benefits to be Reen in the well ordered lives and conduct of those who are true
Masons at heart, as well as in the homes made bright and happy by its influence ; its
kind and charitable dispensations, falling on the worthy like the gentle 1lew of
Heaven, are seen and read "in the trembling lip that fails to Hpeak its thanks and
the crystal tear resting on the eye of gratitude."
This history, these noble deeds and enduring works, all these glorious recollections, are to be still further perpetuatctl and illustrated by ns, if we are true to
Masonry that was, and to Masom·y that shall follow ns. But to-day, I do not desire to
content myself with prying far back into the mist of' ages for the antiquity of Masonry,
to review its past glories, and then urge upon all Masons, as the extent of' MaRomy, a
compliance with its rituals, and strict fulfilment of the re<Jlliremcnts of the great law
of brotherhood alone. 'rhese, my brethren, »!though obligations on us as Mason",
a.re not all that we owe to ourselves or to Masonry.
What, then, is Masonry, and what its mission on earth'! Its foundation is surely
<livine. No wisdom, short of that given especially by Omniscience, could have so
framed an organization that it Bhould outlive principalities and powers, anu all other
societies and associations; that, as century rollc<l after century, and age and gen er·
tion followed close upon age and generation, it should but increase with its age, arnl
strengthen with the lapse of time. All other associations, all other monuments of
human skill, or wisdom, or knowledge, have been transient and transitory; they
lived and they passed away; the place that once knew them knows them no more; but
Masonry, in all ages, in all climes, still the same, unchanging anu unchangeable, haH
endured and pressed on to the final fulfilment of the mission assigneu it by Gou himself at its outset.
Man, created pure, and endowed with all the attributes necessary for his earthly
happiness, had wandered from the path of his God, had violated his solemn oruinances, had brought sin and death into the world. Yes, quickly following his disobeuicnce, crime succeeded crime, in still increasing magnitude, until murder and fratricide
stained the world with a brother's blood: -the trail of the serpent had passed over
all that was pure and happy, and left its blighting, withering curse behind.
That man might not be wholly lost, the bounteous Father of the Universe left him
still with memory to recall the bright and glorious visions of Paradise, when he
walked in Eden with his God, and inculcated in his mind living principles of morality
and right. He taught him their necessities, their beauty and their worth, and clotheu
them for him in attractive hues. Man saw and hoped. God and His angels encouraged the hope, and implanted in his breast the love of those principles of morality
aud virtue which by His grace and blessing have since increased and flourished, and
are now the foundation of Masonry and the root of all good.
As meu increased iu knowledge and in social intercourse, they taught these principles to one another, and associated together that they might thereby be encour.

aged in the practice thereof. l"rom this sprang societies, and, as time passed on, and
God again communicated with His creatures, these a~sociations took upon th.em
shape, until they finally culminated in Ancient Craft Masonry, that Fraternity which
we all revere. It however is but the body, the exemplification of those cardinal
principles. They lay at the foundation of our Order, at the foundation of religion;
and without them, we can neither be happy here, nor hope for happiness hereafter.
These are the tea0hings of )Iasonry. Belief in the immortality, eternity, and
goodness of God, and in man's accountability to Him. That as God is immortal, so is
the soul of man immortal, and that only by strict aclherence to the moral law and
through the grace of God, can he hope for happiness hereafter. As Masons, in God
we must put our trust, and in one only Goel believe, and have encluring faith in the
sacredness and divine inspiration of the Scriptui·es. I care not who, having passed
the outer door of ~fasoury, has witnessed its solemn ceremonial and learned its hidden
arcana, if his heart he not enlightened and illumine cl and his action controlled by a belief in these things, he is not a Mason, neither indeed can he be.
These are they which constitute }fasonry. Its forms and ceremonies are but tbe
symbolic representatives of its reality, ancl in a knowledge of their representation of
these princip!es should all Masons be versed. Believing llrmly and implicitly in, and
ever having present in our minds, the otrict accountability we owe to God, we will
necessarily and naturally desire to !eat! virtuous, benevolent, and upright lh·es; and
as we view His bounteous goodness towards us, and His alrnndant charity towards
all of our transgression•, our hearts will warm with brotherly love towards all mankind ;. and the humble prayer to Him, "to forgive ns our trespasses, as we forgive
those that trespass against us,'' will have a force, a significance, and a pathos we
have never before imagined.
Masonry has been made the custodian of noble and sacred truths, and piously
have they been trarnmiitted froru generation to generation; sometimes recognized
and manifest in all their \Jeanty and purity; and at all times diffusing their benign
influence over its vo1aries. As we look through the various symbols of our Order
and at the t111ths by them illustrated, each step in Masonry seems pointed by the
unerring hand of Deity to lead us on to Hirn. New beauties ever appear clustering
thick around us; the Order and its ceremonials clad in new attractions; and time
itself seems too short to learn all its delights. These forms and ceremonial observances, beautiful and impressive even to the uninstructed Mason, when viewed by
the light of knowledge, impress still more upon our minds tbe divine wisdom which
inspired them.
When, as Entered Apprentices, we first enter the Lodge, we are solemnly taught
the inevitabe punishment of sin, as well as our own blind and helpless condition.
We learn to bow to 'Jod in prayer in times of trouble and trial and allliction-to
invoke His blessings upon al1 our nndertakings, and ei-er remember our dependence
npon Him. We le>!rn the necessity of a virtuous and upright life, and pure and spot·
less reputation. We are taught our duty to ourselves und to our fellow man.
Through the view of the world t1round us, our attention ii! pointed to its great Ruler
and Architect, and we are instructed to have" faith in Him, hope in immortality, and
charity toward all men ;" thus teaching us to live uprightly and, walking truthfully
'i-nd with all humility seeking Divine aid, to so fashion our lives as, despite our rude
and imperfect state by nature, shall fit us for a place in the temple 011 high-being
ever in life full of truth, rtnn in the right, prudent, temperate, and just.
Progressing in the science as J<'ellow Crafts, we still further learn our dependence
upon God, and at all time> to think and speak of Him with due revereme and veuer·
ation; and also th;tt, a:; Ma8ons, we must improve the talent intrusted to our keeping, and so cultivate our miuds and understandings as to exalt our Maker in ennobling
ourselves.
As Master Masons, the full beauty of ancient Masonry is displayed to us in the

most impreesive lessons. Here we learn fidelity, and pure and unfaltering adherence
to truth; that for no temporary benefit or good. nor for safety from threatened harm,
are we to deviate from the right. The neophyte here finds himself surrounded hy
the signs and tokens of death. lt is even itself present with him, and all its dread
paraphernalia cling close to his form and is realized in his peroon. Hut he also learns
thllt, though the" wicked for a time prevail,'' the time will come when a just aml
terrible punishment shall tleseeud upon their gnilty heads. He lem·ns to look without
fear upon rleath and the grave, for through our mystic symbols he looks \Jeyond the
tomb, and se1>s the life prepared for the just and good. He has impressed upon him
anew and hl5tingly the immortality of the mu!, and has manifested to him 1he raising
and restoration of the body, firmly believillf.( that, in the great day when the Builder
shall call for his workmen, it will rise and be as immortal and incorruptible as his
soul--a lesson and a thought that fills onr minds with hope for the future and an earnest
rlesire to fit ourselves for the glorious life opening before us ; that in these bodies
made incorruptible and cleanHerl from every taint of sin, we shall meet, in that other
and better world, the loved and lost that liave gone before ns.
Well may we, as fa1tered Apprentices, be taught to preserve a purity of life and
conversation - well as Fellow Crnfts, to revere Uod -and well, as Master ::liasons,
earnestly to search for and piously preserve the ashes of our deceusecl brother; well
knowing that the body we reverently lay in the tomb •httll he with us clothed again
with life, in the clay when mortality shall put on immortality, and corruption shall
have put on incorruption.
These are the teachings of Masonry brought to onr view hy Rymholic emblems
expressive of them all; e,~ery sign a!Hl symbol, each word and token, conveying
some moral, some divine teaching filled with the preceptH of virtue. To be a Mason
at heat·t is indeed to be a good man and true, renouncing all false gods and all
infidelity.
Thi> being the end and mission of }Iasonry--to inculcate theoe t"'1chings-l10w
manifest the wi"'lom that estah!bhed it, that thereby truths anil historical lessons
might point the mind tu the real aim of life, and impreHci HJJOn it, through signs and
mysteries, the great teachings of Freemasonry, which are the teachings of the Holy
Bible -the eternity aud self·existencc of God-His omniscience and omnipotence antl the rich honors laid np uy Ilim for the Mason in trnt.h. Masonry teaches all this,
and her teachings are true, for they 11re drnwn from the fountain of truth-· the Woril
of Go1l itself.
Thus before W' stands our Masonic edifice in all its simple gnmdeur and greatness:
worthy of its Mttker, God, worthy of its great exemplars, Solomon, Jliram of Tyre,
and Hiram the widow's son, as well as of the love awl adoration of its votaries to tlie
latest day. I•'it is it that its mission should be the noblest ever intrusted to merely
human harnls-to !'ldieve the widow, the poor, and the fatherless- to bind up the
wounds of the sore and the sick-to pour the oil ol'consohttirm upon the bruisctl and
weary spirit---arnl, after making man happier here, to point him to a bright a11il
shining home on high.
The material 'l'emple built by Solomon aud the CruJt at ,Jerusalem fell under the
attacks of its foes. The seconll temple, rebuilt hy the Craft, bas long since passed
away, and even the foundation stones thereof cannot be found. But our Masonic
Temple is but approaching ito completion-its foundation laid broad and deep in the
belief in Deity-its columns each iuscribed with a virtue that smpm;scsthe otherits towers reaching to heaven-its ample space tilled with gooclncss, with purity, and
with truth. Brotherly love pervades its worshipers, and that divine charity, which
ever airls the erring to return, omd forgives the contrite and repentant, IJreathes
through all its votaries.
Grand and majestic Temple! When its fires were dimmed and its altars well nigh
overthrown, its enemies knew that its God still lived, for they could ever read
